reason: The sources provide rich, verified details across multiple sites describing Betelgeuse's runaway velocity, bow shock, physical scale, and dynamic history.
story: Betelgeuse, the glowing red shoulder of Orion, is not staying put. Flung outward from its stellar nursery near Orion's Belt millions of years ago, this colossal red supergiant is an interstellar runaway hurtling through space at 30 kilometers per second. As it plows through interstellar gas, it produces a mammoth bow shock several light-years wide. Bloated to hundreds of times the size of our Sun, Betelgeuse would swallow Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars if dropped into our solar system. Yet this giant is burning through its fuel at breakneck speed. At only ten million years old, it is already approaching its death and is expected to detonate in a supernova within roughly 100,000 years. When it spewed plasma that cooled into dust during the Great Dimming of 2019, skywatchers wondered if the end had arrived. When it finally detonates, it will shine during the day, completely harmless to Earth.
angle: Orion's bright shoulder star is actually a runaway giant plowing through the cosmos at 30 kilometers per second, leaving a bow shock light-years wide.

claims.claim: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant star located in the constellation Orion.
Betelgeuse is a runaway star that was ejected from its birthplace near Orion's Belt.
Betelgeuse moves through the interstellar medium at a speed of 30 kilometers per second (approximately 18.6 miles per second).
Betelgeuse's motion through the interstellar medium creates a massive bow shock.
If placed at the center of the Solar System, Betelgeuse would swallow the orbits of Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.
Betelgeuse is a young star, estimated to be roughly 10 million years old (or between 8.5 and 10 million years old).
Betelgeuse is expected to end its life in a supernova explosion within roughly 100,000 years.
When Betelgeuse explodes as a supernova, life on Earth will be unharmed.
When Betelgeuse explodes, the supernova will be visible during the day for months.
In October 2019, Betelgeuse began dimming noticeably in an event known as the Great Dimming.
During the dimming event, Betelgeuse dropped from among the top 10 brightest stars in the night sky to outside the top 20.
The Great Dimming was caused by ejected superhot plasma that cooled into an obscuring dust cloud.
By early 2020, Betelgeuse stopped fading and began brightening again.
Ancient Chinese astronomers recorded Betelgeuse as a yellow star, before Ptolemy recorded it as orange centuries later.
Betelgeuse's distance from Earth is estimated in the range of 400 to 600 light-years.
The asteroid 319 Leona was predicted to occult Betelgeuse in December 2023, visible along a path crossing Florida and Mexico.

disputed: Diameter of the bow shock: S1 and S2 describe it as roughly four light-years wide, whereas S3 states the diameter is about three light-years. A script should state 'three to four light-years wide'.

Origin of the traditional Arabic name: S1 and S6 attribute it to 'the hand of Orion' (Yad al-Jawza), while S2 states it may derive from 'the armpit of Orion' (Ibt al-Jawza). A script should say 'translated as the hand or armpit of Orion'.

Supernova peak brightness: S1 states it will shine as bright as the half-Moon, S5 states half as bright as the full Moon, and S6 states it will blaze brighter than the full moon. A script should describe it generally as 'rivaling the Moon in the night sky'.

Estimated distance: S1 and S2 cite 400 to 600 light-years (with refined models around 548 light-years), S3 gives roughly 640 light-years, and S7 gives roughly 700 light-years. A script should attribute distance as 'roughly 500 to 600 light-years away'.
